questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A historical explanation offered as the only reading
questions.learningObjective: Identify the weakness in a single-cause historical reading
questions.stem: During handover on the medical ward, a nurse says an older poem can only be read as a protest against one tax. Which objection best weakens her claim?

options.text: One historical cause cannot account for a text shaped by several pressures at once.
The plain wording of a poem always settles meaning more firmly than history does.
options.misconception: believes literal wording settles meaning on its own

options.text: A poem must always be dated before the event it appears to protest.
options.misconception: assumes a text cannot answer its own present

options.text: Only readers who lived through the period can grasp what the poem was doing.
options.misconception: treats historical distance as unreadability

questions.explanation: One cause rarely exhausts a text, which answers several pressures at once, including form and audience. Treating it as the only reading also shuts out evidence a reader could check.
questions.hint: Ask what the single-cause claim leaves no room for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Meaning as a meeting of text and reader
questions.learningObjective: Explain meaning as an encounter between text and reader
questions.stem: At the change of shift, the charge nurse asks why a poem read in a staff room moved one colleague to tears while another called it sentimental. Explain what is being asked of the reader here.

answer.exemplar: The question treats meaning as an encounter rather than a property of the page. The poem supplies constraints, images and a tone, but the feeling it produces is completed by the reader's own history, mood and willingness to be moved, which is why the same lines land differently on two colleagues. The nurse should not be asked to find the single approved reaction, only to describe what the poem makes available and what each reader brought to it.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for an account of reading as a meeting of text and reader, not a hunt for a hidden meaning. Two colleagues differing is evidence for the idea, not a problem to be solved.
questions.hint: Focus on what each reader contributes to the poem.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two accounts of the same effect
questions.learningObjective: Compare two explanations of a single observed effect
questions.stem: Two staff nurses disagree about the same line: one blames the printer's diction, the other the printer's timing. Which account best explains the shared effect they both observed?

options.text: The rhyme scheme forces every reader toward a single approved feeling about the image.
options.misconception: believes form can dictate a reader's response

options.text: Two distinct causes, diction and timing, can produce the same effect without either being the whole story.
A shared effect proves that one cause must be dominant and the other merely incidental.
options.misconception: treats convergence as proof of a single cause

options.text: The effect is best explained by the general mood of the ward on that particular afternoon.
options.misconception: explains a textual effect by a passing circumstance

questions.explanation: Two accounts can explain one effect without either being the whole story, since distinct causes often converge on the same result. Insisting on one dominant cause misreads convergence as proof.
questions.hint: Convergent causes do not need one to be the whole truth.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The lens a colonial reading applies
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the gains and limits of a colonial interpretive lens
questions.stem: In the rest area, a junior nurse says a travel narrative is about empire and nothing else. Build the strongest two-sentence reply, including what the reading contributes and what it leaves out.

options.text: The reading is wrong because the writer never mentions the empire or any of its officials.
options.misconception: requires a text to name its subject explicitly

options.text: The reading is weak because the writer's account of distant places shows no interest in its reader.
options.misconception: judges a text by its engagement with readers

options.text: The reading usefully foregrounds power and exchange but narrows the text if it becomes the only lens.
The reading is strong because historical context always tells us more about a text than it does.
options.misconception: assumes context outranks the text itself

questions.explanation: A colonial lens can illuminate power and exchange while still narrowing the text. The best reply accepts the lens's contribution and states the cost of treating it as exhaustive.
questions.hint: Name both the gain and the loss.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A colonial reading that mistakes circulation for agreement
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish circulation of a text from agreement with it

stimulus.body: The pamphlet was reprinted in four cities and bound into cloth for sale at nineteen pence. Everyone I have asked agrees it was a rallying text. Surely that means its readers approved of what it said.

questions.stem: The agency nurse reading this comment asks what the evidence about print runs actually establishes. Which reading is most defensible?

options.text: Print runs show that a text was widely available, and nothing at all about how readers responded.
options.misconception: overcorrects by denying that reception can be studied

options.text: Because the pamphlet was sold cheaply, the people who bought it must have wanted radical change.
options.misconception: infers belief from the price of a book

options.text: Sales figures are the clearest measure of the agreement a text won from its readers.
options.misconception: treats a commercial record as a record of conviction

options.text: Wide circulation shows the text reached many readers, but circulation alone does not show agreement.

questions.explanation: Circulation is evidence of reach and of a market, not of approval. A text can be bought for curiosity, collection or pressure, so treating wide sale as consent confuses availability with response.
questions.hint: Availability and agreement are different kinds of evidence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison organised by a held-constant question
questions.learningObjective: Construct a comparison that holds one question constant
questions.stem: During a busy handover in the surgical ward, two colleagues want to compare two poems from different centuries and cannot agree on a method. Set out how to build a comparison that holds one question constant.

answer.exemplar: A workable comparison starts by fixing the question before choosing the texts, for example how each poem represents an absence. Both passages are then read for the same features, such as who is addressed, what is withheld and how the ending resolves, and claims are compared feature by feature. This keeps the comparison fair, because the same questions are put to each text instead of one text being mined for strengths and the other for deficits.

questions.explanation: A held-constant question means both texts answer the same demand, so the comparison tests a difference rather than a preference. Choosing texts first produces two unrelated summaries.
questions.hint: Fix the question before choosing the passages.

options.misconception: reverses the two terms

options.text: Theme and chronology are two names for the same organising principle of a literary work.
options.misconception: collapses two distinct enquiries into one

options.text: Theme measures how many sections a work has, while chronology measures how long each section runs.
options.misconception: confuses a principle with a structural measurement

questions.explanation: Theme concerns the preoccupations a work returns to; chronology concerns sequence. Confusing the two makes a thematic point look like a narrative fact and hides what comparison would reveal.
questions.hint: One term is about concerns, the other about order.

options.misconception: repeats the premise instead of testing it

options.text: Political pressure may leave no obvious trace while still shaping a text's occasion, form and restraint.

options.misconception: requires influence to be explicit to count

options.text: The manager's conclusion depends on how much the poem charms the listener, not on the text.
options.misconception: judges a historical claim by personal impression

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Meaning as a meeting of text and reader
questions.learningObjective: Apply the encounter model of meaning to two readers
questions.stem: While updating the board, a nurse asks how a line can mean one thing to her and another to a colleague from a different background. Explain the reading process in terms she can use with the patient group.

answer.exemplar: The line carries a fixed textual form, a vocabulary and an arrangement, but what it does to a reader depends on experience brought from outside the poem. The nurse should describe the two readings as products of that meeting: her own reading draws on associations and history the colleague does not share, while the colleague's draws on different ones. Neither reading is idle or false; each is the poem working through a particular reader.

questions.explanation: The question wants meaning as an encounter between a text's features and a reader's experience. Answering that it is simply subjective would abandon the text's constraints.
questions.hint: Keep the text's constraints and the reader's input together.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two accounts of the same effect
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise competing accounts of one literary effect
questions.stem: At midnight handover in the intensive care unit, a nurse asks whether a single passage can be explained by metre alone or by print conventions alone. Construct the answer that respects both accounts.

options.text: The metre reading is right because sound lies nearer to the surface of a poem than any material fact.
options.misconception: privileges one level of explanation by proximity alone

options.text: The print conventions reading is right because metre tells us nothing about who printed a poem.
options.misconception: assumes a dimension of the text carries no evidence

options.text: Both accounts identify real features that could produce the effect, and each alone leaves it unexplained.
Neither account is adequate, since the effect is best treated as accidental and needs no cause.
options.misconception: treats a pattern as the absence of a cause

questions.explanation: A careful answer names what each explanation covers and what it leaves out rather than picking a winner by assertion. If both accounts are partial, the effect has more than one cause.
questions.hint: Say what each account explains and what it misses.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The lens a colonial reading applies
questions.learningObjective: Describe how an interpretive lens organises attention

stimulus.body: The ward keeps a laminated card of reading recommendations that came from the hospital's founding charity. Someone added a note in pen: read them as a colonist would, that is, as a way of taking possession. Is that the only way to read them?

questions.stem: The newly qualified nurse asks how the colonial lens shapes what the laminated card can tell us. Which claim about the lens is most accurate?

options.text: A colonial lens is a false reading and should be discarded once better scholarship arrives.
options.misconception: dismisses a lens rather than testing its limits

options.text: The lens is neutral, since every reader arrives with a frame of some kind.
options.misconception: calls a lens neutral and so exempt from scrutiny

options.text: The lens only applies to texts written before the colonial period it describes.
options.misconception: restricts a reading method to one historical window

options.text: The lens foregrounds power and possession but can distort the text if it becomes the only way of reading.

questions.explanation: The lens is a revealing frame for texts shaped by imperial contact, but it selects and emphasises. The useful question is what it reveals and what a reader can check about its limits.
questions.hint: Ask what a lens reveals and what it hides.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A colonial reading that mistakes circulation for agreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain why attendance is not evidence of endorsement
questions.stem: In the handover brief, the sister reports that a lecture hall was packed for a colonial address. The student asks why a full hall is being treated as proof that the audience agreed.

answer.exemplar: A full lecture hall shows that an audience assembled and stayed, which is a fact about attendance and attention rather than about belief. People fill seats for many reasons, including reputation, curiosity, obligation or the wish to argue later, and the published minutes may record only applause from a friendly section. The honest inference is that the address reached an audience; what they made of it has to be argued from other evidence such as letters, later citation or changes in local practice.

questions.explanation: Attendance and endorsement are separate kinds of evidence. Treating a crowd as consent mistakes an event's visibility for its content.
questions.hint: Attendance is not the same as agreement.

questions.topic: A comparison organised by a held-constant question

options.text: Choose the two most famous poems, since reputation settles which comparison matters most.
options.misconception: chooses significance in place of a question

options.text: Hold one question constant, then examine how each poem answers that same question.
Choose two poems written in the same decade, since dates make comparison straightforward.
options.misconception: substitutes shared circumstance for shared question

options.text: Read each poem on its own first, then select the point of contact that seems most striking.
options.misconception: lets convenience pick the point of contact

questions.explanation: Holding the question constant makes the comparison test something specific rather than collect two readings side by side. Reputation and shared dates introduce interests that can drift from it.
questions.hint: The same question must be put to both poems.

questions.topic: Two principles compared, theme against chronology
questions.learningObjective: Relate theme and chronology without collapsing them
questions.stem: Over a quiet night shift, the handover question is whether a work's theme and its chronology can be compared at all. Which answer handles the relation between them properly?

options.text: They cannot be compared, because one belongs to the content of a work and the other to its structure.
options.misconception: severs the two enquiries as incomparable in principle

options.text: They can be compared, but only if the theme is restated as a sequence of events first.
options.misconception: reduces one enquiry to the other before comparing

options.text: They answer different questions and can still be set against each other on the same text.
Chronology always reveals the theme, so the two are two names for the same enquiry.
options.misconception: assumes sequence settles meaning

questions.explanation: Theme and chronology ask different questions of a work, which is why setting them against each other can be revealing: one shows what recurs, the other what follows. Merging them removes the contrast.
questions.hint: Different questions can still be set against each other.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A historical explanation offered as the only reading
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a single-cause historical account omits
questions.stem: In the handover to the day team, a nurse argues that only the political climate can explain why a pamphlet appeared when it did. Explain what is missing from her account.

answer.exemplar: Her account isolates one pressure, the political climate, and treats it as a sufficient cause for the pamphlet's date and shape. What is missing is the range of other determining factors: the author's particular situation, the demands of a small format, the availability of a printer, the audience the pamphlet was written for and the conventions of pamphlet writing. These are not alternatives to historical explanation but its necessary detail, and without them the explanation cannot be tested against the text.

questions.explanation: The gap is the range of non-political causes the pamphlet's form, audience and making also depend on. A historical reading becomes convincing when it accounts for such details.
questions.hint: Name the practical conditions the single cause ignores.

questions.topic: Meaning as a meeting of text and reader
questions.learningObjective: Balance the reader's contribution against the text's constraints
questions.stem: On the long-stay ward, a nurse says patients take from a poem exactly what they bring to it. Which conclusion best balances what is true in that remark and what it leaves out?

options.misconception: denies the text any authority over interpretation

options.text: The remark is right, since meaning is fixed entirely by the reader's state of mind at the time.
options.misconception: reduces meaning to a single momentary state

options.text: The remark is wrong, since poems produce their own meanings and readers only receive them.
options.misconception: removes the reader from the account entirely

options.text: The remark catches the reader's contribution but understates the constraints the text imposes.

questions.explanation: A reader brings experience, but a poem also constrains what can be read and in what order. The balanced conclusion keeps both, which is why the remark is half right rather than simply right.
questions.hint: Keep the reader's input and the text's limits.

questions.learningObjective: Handle two competing accounts of one effect in a record

questions.stem: The night sister asks how the two notes should be handled in the handover. Which course of action is most defensible?

options.text: Record both as possible causes and say what evidence would distinguish them.
File the note with the stronger-sounding explanation and discard the other for clarity.
options.misconception: prefers the more confident account over the better one

options.misconception: treats a literary question as outside the record's scope

questions.explanation: Two accounts of one effect can both be right in part, so the useful move is to keep both and name the evidence that would separate them. Discarding one for tidiness avoids the question.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The lens a colonial reading applies
questions.learningObjective: Trace how a lens changes which evidence counts
questions.stem: Before the ward round, the sister asks the team to describe how a colonial reading changes what counts as evidence in an old account. Answer in a way the team can check.

answer.exemplar: A colonial reading tends to foreground encounters between peoples, trade, land, labour and authority, and it treats those as the passage's main subject rather than as background. That choice changes the evidence the reader privileges: maps, ledgers, official correspondence and travel reports gain weight, while domestic detail, comic passages and ordinary labour may be read as ornament. The team should notice this by asking which parts of the account become invisible once the lens is in place, and whether that invisibility is the lens's blind spot or the text's genuine emphasis.

questions.explanation: The reply must show the lens acting on the evidence rather than on the mood, by tracing what a reader counts as significant. A general statement about bias cannot be checked.
questions.hint: Trace what the lens makes the reader count as evidence.

options.misconception: reads acceptance out of a printing history

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two principles compared, theme against chronology
questions.learningObjective: Design a method for setting theme against chronology
questions.stem: For the night staff, a nurse asks how a theme and a sequence of events can be examined in one sitting. Set out a method she can use with the team.

answer.exemplar: The method is to treat the two as two separate passes over the same text and then bring them together. First the nurse records the concerns the text keeps returning to, noting where and how often each recurs without worrying about order. Second she sets out the sequence of events as the text presents it, with dates where these can be established from the text or its context. Only after both passes are complete does she set the theme against the chronology, asking whether the sequence of events supports, complicates or contradicts what the work keeps returning to.

questions.explanation: A workable method keeps the two enquiries distinct until there is something to compare, which prevents one being forced to illustrate the other. The final step asks what the relation shows.
questions.hint: Run two separate passes, then set them against each other.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two accounts of the same effect
questions.learningObjective: Explain how distinct causes can converge on one change
questions.stem: The handover mentions that a paragraph's tone changed after a printer swapped a repeated word for a plainer one. Explain why two separate causes might still be credited with the change.

answer.exemplar: The swap altered the sound and rhythm the reader hears, while the printer's decision also belonged to a workshop practice that affected how the book was presented and sold. Because these are different kinds of cause, one operating on the page as read and one on the material conditions of the book, both can be credited with the change in tone without one cancelling the other. The nurse should describe the effects as overlapping rather than as rival explanations, and note what evidence would show which contributed more.

questions.explanation: Distinct causes acting at different levels can converge on a single observed change. Treating convergence as a contest is what leads people to dismiss a genuine second explanation.
questions.hint: Overlapping causes can produce one visible result.

answer.exemplar: The test is whether the question can be put to both texts in the same form, using features that each text genuinely possesses, and whether answering it would show a difference worth explaining. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Meaning as a meeting of text and reader
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two readings can share one text
questions.stem: The outgoing nurse is asked to describe how two readers can both be right about a poem and yet be reading the same words. Write the explanation she would give at handover.

answer.exemplar: Both readers are working on the same words, so the text constrains them equally, and each is not free to read anything at all. What differs is the material they bring: the associations, memories and judgements that make one phrase land as tenderness and another as threat. The poem performs the same set of operations for each reader, but those operations land differently because the reader completes them. That is why the difference between the readings is informative about the poem and about its audience, rather than a sign that someone has misread it.

questions.explanation: The explanation must hold two things at once: readers are constrained by the words, and their completions differ. Dropping either half produces pure subjectivism or determinism.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why wide readership and agreement are confused
questions.stem: The tutor asks students to explain why a wide readership and a widespread agreement are often confused in accounts of a text's influence. Write an answer that could be used in an essay.

answer.exemplar: Readers are scattered in time, place and interest, and the numbers we can count rarely reach the reasons they read. A text may circulate widely because it was cheap, taught, required or fashionable, and each of these conditions has its own logic that is indifferent to the text's claims. Agreement is a claim about what thousands of separated readers concluded, and almost no document records it directly. Influence therefore has to be argued from reception, citation, parody and the uses people actually made of a text, not inferred from its print run.

questions.explanation: The confusion arises because both are measured by numbers, but one measures distribution and the other conviction. An essay answer should separate the counts and name better evidence.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a date does and does not establish
questions.stem: At the handover to the morning team, a nurse explains why saying a poem was written in a particular year does not by itself tell us what it means. Write what she would say.

answer.exemplar: The date fixes a text in a set of circumstances: what was in circulation, what form was available, which events had just happened and who could read it. Those circumstances shape what a writer could and would attempt, so a date is a genuine condition of a text. It does not settle meaning, because the same year produced texts of very different purposes and the same circumstances left different writers free to respond in different ways. The date is where the inquiry begins, not where it ends.

questions.explanation: The date is a condition of the text and a starting point for enquiry, not a conclusion about meaning. Texts from one year differ widely, so a date constrains without deciding.

answer.exemplar: The lens sets a prior question before reading begins: how does this account organise encounters between peoples and lands, and who benefits from the arrangement it describes? With that question in view, certain passages come forward, such as accounts of trade, travel and authority, while others recede, including domestic detail, humour and the labour that makes the journey possible. The nurse's task is then to notice that recession and to ask whether it follows from the text's own emphases or only from the lens the reader brought to it.

answer.exemplar: The brief should set out the two enquiries separately first: one pass records what the work keeps returning to, another records what happens and in what order, with dates only where the text or its context supports them. questions.explanation: The answerable framing puts both accounts to the same evidence and asks whether it explains the same facts. Preference, seniority and a sense of the fitting settle the question without inquiry.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The lens a colonial reading applies
questions.learningObjective: Describe emphasis using shape and pacing as well as content

stimulus.body: The old account mentions a market, a river crossing and a dispute over land, and it gives the trader three days of greetings before the reader learns his business. Someone says the account is therefore only about trade.

questions.stem: The sister asks how the account's emphasis should be described. Which reading is most defensible?

options.text: The account is only about trade, since the greeting days form the bulk of the surviving text.
options.misconception: infers thematic weight from sheer length alone

options.text: Trade structures the account, but its shape and pacing show the writer's priorities extend beyond trade.
The account is not about trade at all, since the market is mentioned only in passing.
options.misconception: dismisses a repeated concern because it is mentioned briefly

options.text: The account is equally about every subject it mentions, so no emphasis can be claimed.
options.misconception: insists on a total equivalence that cannot be checked

questions.explanation: The account's shape gives trade a real place while the detail it spends elsewhere shows a writer with other priorities in view. Relative length alone does not settle emphasis.
questions.hint: Look at shape and pacing, not just mention.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A colonial reading that mistakes circulation for agreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an anthology reveals about its compilers
questions.stem: Students are asked why an anthology assembled abroad tells us about editors more than about readers. Write the explanation they should give.

answer.exemplar: An anthology records choices made by someone with particular interests, connections and access, and those choices determine which texts were available to readers at all. The selection therefore carries the editor's judgement about what was worth preserving, and that judgement can be studied directly by asking which kinds of work appear and which do not. What the volume cannot show is how its readers responded, since presence in a volume records inclusion rather than admiration, and silence records an editorial decision rather than a reader's rejection.

questions.explanation: Inclusion in a volume is evidence of an editor's selection, and absence is evidence of an editor's choice, so the volume speaks most clearly about its compilers. Response requires other documents.
questions.hint: Inclusion records an editor's judgement.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison organised by a held-constant question
questions.learningObjective: Select the fairest arrangement for comparing two accounts
questions.stem: The team must compare two accounts that describe the same journey. Which arrangement of the method gives the fairest result?

options.text: Compare the accounts on whatever aspect each one makes easiest to describe first.
options.misconception: lets convenience choose the point of comparison

options.text: Compare the longer account with the shorter, treating the difference in length as the main finding.
options.misconception: mistakes extent for a comparative finding

options.text: Choose the account with more reliable dates, since that account can then stand alone.
options.misconception: privileges one text and abandons the comparison

options.text: Fix one question, put it to both accounts, then compare the two sets of answers.

questions.explanation: A fixed question applied in the same form to both accounts is what makes a difference a finding rather than an accident of the material. Convenience, length and dating all replace the comparison.
questions.hint: One question, both accounts, then compare.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two principles compared, theme against chronology
questions.learningObjective: Defend the possibility of comparing two different enquiries
questions.stem: The sister asks whether a thematic reading and a chronological reading can be set against each other in a single discussion. Which reply is most careful?

options.text: Yes, provided both are carried out on the same text before either is used to explain the other.
Yes, provided the thematic reading is set first, since it is the more revealing of the two.
options.misconception: prejudges the comparison by ranking the enquiries first

options.text: No, because one of the two readings always turns out to be the text's real meaning.
options.misconception: assumes only one enquiry can be legitimate

options.text: No, because the two readings ask questions that cannot be asked of the same text.
options.misconception: mistakes two enquiries for incompatible ones

questions.explanation: The two readings can be set against each other as long as each is completed on its own terms first, which prevents one being read into the other. Ranking one as superior prejudges the comparison.
questions.hint: Complete both separately before comparing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A historical explanation offered as the only reading
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a date establishes and leaves open
questions.stem: The handover asks the nurse to explain why the date a poem was written is one piece of evidence rather than the answer to what it means. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The date tells the reader what was available and expected when the poem was made, and poems written in the same year can be as different as the years that separate them. A date is evidence about the conditions of writing, and it makes certain questions good ones to ask, such as whether the poem answers an immediate occasion. It is not a key that unlocks a fixed meaning, because the same conditions permitted many different and incompatible purposes, and only the text can say which one it took.

questions.explanation: The explanation must treat the date as a condition and an occasion for questions, not a key to fixed meaning. Texts from one year differ widely, so the date narrows possibilities.
questions.hint: A date is a condition and an occasion, not a key.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Meaning as a meeting of text and reader
questions.learningObjective: Combine the text's shape with the reader's force
questions.stem: The team must answer a patient who insists the poem means only what she feels it means. Which reply best combines what the poem gives and what she brings?

options.text: Your feeling is the reading, and the poem's words add nothing further to it.
options.misconception: makes the reader's response the whole of the reading

options.text: The words give the reading its shape, and your own experience gives it its particular force.
The words are fixed and your feeling is a mistake that a better reader would avoid.
options.misconception: treats a feeling as an error to be corrected

options.text: Only the original reader's feeling counts, so later readers cannot make the poem mean anything.
options.misconception: restricts valid reading to the first audience

questions.explanation: The balanced reply credits the text with the structure and the reader with the response, which is why the feeling is neither everything nor nothing. Each extreme denies one half of a reading.
questions.hint: Shape from the words, force from the reader.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two accounts of the same effect
questions.learningObjective: Treat two supported accounts as testable propositions

stimulus.body: Reading room note. The first explanation says the passage became famous because it was printed on the back of a broadsheet that was itself widely bought. The second says it became famous because people recognised a situation it described. Both explanations match the evidence we have.

questions.stem: The librarian asks how the two explanations should be treated. Which judgement is best?

options.text: One must be the true account, since the evidence cannot support two explanations at once.
options.misconception: assumes a single explanation by default

options.text: The evidence is inadequate, so the note should be withdrawn from the reading room record.
options.misconception: discards supported accounts rather than refining them

options.text: They describe different aspects of the same process and can both be tested against the record.
The second explanation is preferable because audience response matters more than distribution.
options.misconception: ranks explanations by a general preference between causes

questions.explanation: The explanations concern different stages of one process of reception, which is why both can be supported by the same evidence and tested against it. Forcing one to win avoids the inquiry.
questions.hint: Different stages of one process.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The lens a colonial reading applies
questions.learningObjective: Write a handover note on using a lens without a verdict
questions.stem: The outgoing sister must write a handover note on how a colonial reading lens can be used without becoming a verdict. Write the note she would leave.

answer.exemplar: The note should record the lens as a method: it asks what the text does about encounters between peoples, lands and authority, and it makes certain passages legible that a reader focused elsewhere might pass over. It should also record its cost: passages that the text treats as ordinary, including domestic detail, humour and the labour behind the scenes, can sink into background once the lens is in place. A lens used well therefore names what it reveals, flags what it risks hiding, and leaves the reader to test the account against the pages themselves.

questions.explanation: The note must present the lens as a method with gains and costs, not as a conclusion. A note saying only what the lens finds is a verdict; one saying only what it risks is an objection.
questions.hint: Name the gain and the cost in the same note.
